Your take works in a vacuum, but it lacks the nuance of understand what a model is and what constitutes a parameter in that greater context.

>The model is the neural network itself

No, and especially not with these LLMs. If someone handed you the "raw" neural network of a modern LLM, you couldn't just run forward passes through it and expect it to behave the same way a proper agent behaves. This should be obvious, but that's an important distinction. Everything else you need to make that neural network behave like an agent are apart of the overall model that we're talking about here. And any parameter of that "everything else" are effectively parameters of the agent itself.

Think about a model as a function: you give it some input and it produces some output. A simple model could be something literally like a linear function, f(x) = mx + b. Here, you could say f has two parameters: m and b. That all makes sense and "scales" up to neural networks where there's a lot more parameters, but it's basically just a bunch of these functions where the weights are like m and b in the linear function.

But that's not really the full picture for an LLM, right? For example, if you talk about an agent, there inputs you give it would be your prompt and the outputs it produces is whatever text it generates. But what about its system prompt? If that effectively remains fixed, then that's not really an input of the 'function' that is an agent, right? But it does influence the output of the agent. So, from a certain perspective, the system prompt is actually a parameter of the agent. Tweaking that parameter can cause it to produce different outputs for the same input. More importantly, tweaking that parameter can cause it to produce better outputs than it would otherwise. So if you have one agent test another agent by tuning its system prompt such that the output of the second agent is better than it was before, you just had one agent optimize the parameters of another agent. And that's just the system prompt. Think about the overall harness (where the actual codebase can be considered a parameter) or how multiple agents interact with each other and the parameters involved with those kinds of processes.

I'm willing to bet you don't buy that explanation, but I can assure you that in machine learning there is a lot of consideration for the parameters which come outside the actual weights of the model, and tuning those parameters can be just as important as tuning the weights of a neural network. I'll say that understanding and accepting this was one of the most important realizations I had while studying ML.

This is one of the biggest benefits. I'm not a plugin user so I don't remember how they're different from skills. Not speaking about the tool in OP specifically but regarding skills in general: you can have essentially the entire task or some of its subtasks (which you'd ordinarily direct to the agent using the skill, the main benefits of which are clearer natural language directions) handled with assistive tools written in any language your environment supports. You can additionally supply the skill with its own config files, data files, etc., building essentially a small repo within particular skills and making these resources however closely tied to the skill as you prefer.

This is particularly useful when the agent would otherwise be doing a task that is programmable, or the agent is inconsistent or unable to do it in an efficient, performant or other preferred manner. The programmatic tool assistance means at least some parts of the task (possibly its entirety) could be handled in a well-tested and deterministic manner. How reliable the determinism, optimality, etc. are depends on how well you or the agent writes and verifies the code, tests, spec, etc. in the first place of course, but that only needs to be done correctly once.

The other great benefit is reduced token use, potentially a massive reduction. Imagine a task Claude takes 10 minutes to prepare to do because it's reading and analyzing files for the 3rd time in the last 4 minutes, then it's asking for permissions several times in between to do this and that even after you put it in auto mode, then it's "thinking" again for the thousandth time about how to approach the task even though you had it repeat the task a hundred times already...by the time it actually starts doing the task, the most recent models are likely to have churned through tens of thousands of tokens (and that's a conservative estimate for frontier models) in the first 10 minutes. But, with tool assistance, you can have Claude directly handle some parts of that same task which, for example, needs unpredictable analysis or decision-making each time, but also have it use a set of highly optimized programs to handle the bottleneck parts or the parts you want done "your way." You could potentially cut down those 10 minutes of prep time + whatever minutes to actually do the task down to seconds, with barely a couple of thousand tokens used up. Just an example of course, but I've benefited from this strategy repeatedly across various tasks, simple ones and very complex ones.

Another great thing is that the tools don't have to be tied to the skill at all, they can live anywhere in your codebase. You could even manually run the scripts like any other to handle certain tasks in their entirety or do the prep work before setting an agent loose on the remainder. There are many different approaches with different advantages. It's like actually using the agent as your...well, agent! But now you're supplying him with the latest gadgets like M/Q does for 007.
